To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the use of short-course antibiotic therapy, lasting 3 - 7 days, is feasible for the treatment of uncomplicated community-acquired infections in immunocompetents patients with a low bacterial load, and (ii) the use of single-dose therapy is also feasible for some infections.

the development of short antibiotic courses has been facilitated by the availability of new agents, which have a prolonged duration of activity and by pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamics in vitro and animal model data.

(1) the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamics of the antimicrobial agent are critical in determining the efficacy of the short-course antibiotic; and (2) short-course therapy can be successfully applied in the treatment of a number of community-acquired bacterial infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the efficacy of short courses of antibiotics in the treatment of community acquired infections in adults and children.
the development of new short-course antibiotic therapy regimens, and with the identification of those pharmacokinetic parameters that are most important in this respect.
the development of new short-course antibiotic regimens for the treatment of infections in humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
short-course antibiotic therapy is feasible for the treatment of many community-acquired bacterial infections.
the development of new dosing regimens is an important and necessary step in the treatment of infectious diseases.
the use of short-course regimens for the treatment of common community-acquired infections in immunocompetant patients is a viable option.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of short-course antibiotic treatment is feasible for the treatment of a number of common infections in immunocompetant patients.

short-course therapy is feasible in the treatment of a wide variety of infections, including respiratory tract, skin and soft-tissue, bone and joint infections, urinary tract infections, sexually transmitted diseases and gastrointestinal tract infections.

the use of single-dose therapy for the treatment of streptococci, gonococci and Escherichia coli infections is feasible and that short-course dosing for other community-acquired infections is also possible, although the use of longer courses of therapy is still required.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in order to develop new short-course dosings regimens, it is important to identify the parameters that are important in the development of such regimens, such as pharmacodynamic indices, pharmacokinetic/pharmacokinetic parameters, bacterial load, site of infection and pathogen.
the development of resistance can be minimized with the use of short-course antibiotic therapy.
short-course therapy may be feasible in a number of clinical situations, but the choice of antibiotic and the duration of treatment must be tailored to the individual patient.
